What it is
- Latona Township is a civil township (a local unit of rural government) in Walsh County, North Dakota.
- Walsh County is in the Red River Valley of the North, with Grafton as the county seat.

Government and services
- Like other North Dakota townships, it’s typically governed by a three‑member board of supervisors plus a clerk and treasurer.
- Common responsibilities: maintenance of township roads and ditches, some local zoning/land‑use decisions (where not handled at the county level), weed control, and certain rural services coordination.
- Annual township meetings and elections are usually held in March under North Dakota law.
- Law enforcement is provided by the Walsh County Sheriff; fire/EMS are provided by nearby rural fire protection districts and ambulance services based in the nearest towns.

Land, land use, and economy
- Most civil townships in this part of North Dakota cover about 36 square miles (a 6×6‑mile Public Land Survey “township”), though exact shapes can vary with rivers or historical survey exceptions.
- The landscape is generally very flat, part of the former bed of glacial Lake Agassiz, with rich, heavy clay loam soils.
- Land use is overwhelmingly agricultural. Common regional crops include spring wheat, soybeans, corn, sugar beets, barley, sunflowers, and alfalfa; there’s also pasture and hay. Tile drainage and section‑line road ditches are common features.
- Natural features include prairie pothole wetlands and shelterbelts; wildlife typically includes waterfowl, deer, pheasants, and grouse.

Context in Walsh County/region
- Walsh County was organized in 1881 and saw settlement by diverse immigrant communities (notably Norwegian, Polish, and German/Russian heritage), whose cultural footprints remain in churches, cemeteries, and place names.
- Hydrology in the county is dominated by the Park River and Forest River systems flowing east toward the Red River of the North; township drainage generally ties into those systems.
- Rural residents are usually served by nearby school districts headquartered in towns such as Grafton, Park River, Minto, or Midway; students are bused from the township. Exact district coverage depends on current boundary maps.

Population and housing (what’s typical)
- Rural Walsh County townships commonly have populations from a few dozen to a couple hundred residents, with very low density and a mix of farmsteads and rural homes. I don’t have Latona Township’s exact headcount at hand.

Transportation and infrastructure
- Roads generally follow the section‑line grid (every mile), with a mix of gravel township roads and improved county roads; a state highway may be nearby depending on location.
- Utilities include rural electric cooperatives, rural water systems where available, private wells/septic elsewhere, and telephone/broadband via regional providers (coverage varies).

Origin of the name
- Many North Dakota townships adopted classical or settler‑heritage names. “Latona” is another name for Leto from classical mythology; it’s plausible that’s the name’s origin, but I don’t have a definitive source specific to this township.

How to get precise, current details
- Population and housing: U.S. Census Bureau (data.census.gov) — search “Latona township, Walsh County, North Dakota.”
- Legal boundaries and exact location: North Dakota GIS Hub or Walsh County GIS/auditor’s office township maps.
- Feature confirmation: USGS GNIS (search “Latona Township” as a civil feature in Walsh County).
- Roads and services: North Dakota DOT county maps; Walsh County Highway Department.
- School districts: North Dakota Department of Public Instruction boundary maps.
- Land cover/crops: USDA Cropland Data Layer (NASS) and FSA/NRCS resources.
